subject: Access model evaluation for Acme pilot — peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN
messages:
From: Olga Petrov <olga.petrov@redwood.ai>
To: acme-netops@acmecloud.com, Sarah Liu <sarah.liu@acmecloud.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>, Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-11-28T09:12:00-08:00
Subject: Access model evaluation for Acme pilot — peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN

Hi Sarah / Acme NetOps team,

Thanks again for agreeing to the pilot. Before we kick off the lab we wanted to share our recommended access-model options and a quick matrix to help you decide which path to use for the production cutover. Attached is a simple sketch of the pilot topology and a PrivateLink checklist.

High-level tradeoffs we see for your workload (low-latency inference, bursty traffic from web tier, strict audit record requirements):

- VPC peering
  - Pros: lowest latency, simplest from a data plane perspective, straightforward for same-region workloads and when both sides are in AWS.
  - Cons: cross-account routing rules required, no service-endpoint-level access controls (all subnets reachable unless restricted by security groups/NACLs).

- PrivateLink (AWS PrivateLink / interface endpoints)
  - Pros: endpoint-level isolation, egress controlled by service owner, works across accounts/regions with endpoint services, minimal route-table churn. Good fit if you want explicit service-level ACL.
  - Cons: slightly higher per-GB cost, somewhat higher connection setup complexity and requires the endpoint service to be fronted by us.

- Site-to-site VPN (IPsec)
  - Pros: fast to stand up for proof-of-concept, useful as an interim or fallback path, supports non-AWS customer networks easily.
  - Cons: higher latency/jitter, less predictable throughput, operational overhead for long-term (key rotation, monitoring).

Our recommended approach for the pilot: use a dual-path pattern — primary path via VPC peering (same-region low-latency path) with PrivateLink for the control/management APIs and for enforcing tighter ingress for higher-sensitivity models. Keep S2S VPN as a documented fallback for DR/legacy connectivity.

Action items:
- Can you confirm if Acme will accept cross-account peering for the pilot VPC (account ID 987654321)?
- If yes, we’ll share IAM role ARNs and the peering request step-by-step.
- Alternatively, if you prefer endpoint-first, we can provision a PrivateLink endpoint service and share the acceptance flow; that takes ~2 business days to validate on our side.

I’ve CC’d Ben and Kim for cost and security sign-off.

Thanks,
Olga
Lead Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

Olga —

Thanks for the clear summary. A few quick questions from our network/security side:

1) For cross-account peering, will Redwood require route propagation across multiple subnets? We prefer to minimize route-table churn.
2) For PrivateLink, can you confirm what metrics we would need to expose in our VPC network (flow logs, ENI tagging) so our monitoring team can map traffic to the service endpoints?
3) Is there an egress cost estimate you can share for PrivateLink vs peering for ~12TB/month?

Attached is our standard network security questionnaire; I started filling Section 1. We’ll loop in our cloud infra team tomorrow.

—Sarah

From: Olga Petrov <olga.petrov@redwood.ai>

Date: 2026-11-29T08:22:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Access model evaluation for Acme pilot — peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN

Sarah —

Answers inline and a suggested pilot schedule: 

1) Route propagation: the peering setup we propose only requires a small set of explicit route entries for the Redwood subnets that host inference nodes; we won’t ask you to propagate across unrelated subnets. We’ll provide the CIDR blocks to add to two route tables.

2) PrivateLink metrics: exporting VPC Flow Logs + ENI tags is sufficient. We recommend the following fields be enabled: srcaddr, dstaddr, action, protocol, bytes, and interface-id. We’ll provide a short CloudWatch dashboard template you can reuse.

3) Egress estimate: ballpark — PrivateLink data processing + endpoint charges typically add ~0.5–1.0c/GB on our rough workload model; peering has no interface charge but you pay standard data transfer rates (your egress policy may make peering cheaper at scale). For 12TB/month that’s ~USD 60–120/mo differential in our estimate; we’ll run more precise numbers during the pilot.

Suggested pilot timeline:
- Day 0 (alignment): finalize peering vs endpoint choice.
- Day 1–2 (setup): create peering connection OR accept endpoint service + security group rules; exchange IAM role ARNs.
- Day 3 (smoke tests): small-batch inference tests, KV cache validation.
- Day 4–7 (load test): run representative traffic patterns, measure 95th p95 latency and error modes.

If you prefer, we can provision PrivateLink first and run initial smoke tests while peering is set up as the primary path — this is the dual-path approach I mentioned.

I attached the PrivateLink checklist and the pilot topology.

Next step: Sarah — can you indicate a preferred pilot start date (next week looks open on our side)?

Thanks,
Olga

- If PrivateLink is selected, add a per-endpoint surcharge in the pilot invoice to cover endpoint provisioning and monitoring.

Also: Kim, please confirm whether the pilot requires any additional logging retention for compliance. I think Acme asked about audit-level logs for 90 days.
